newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan president promises elections in February.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan president promises elections in February.

text.p: Pakistan's President Farooq Leghari, promising to hold elections on schedule on February 3, said on Thursday his caretaker government had achieved more in five weeks than past governments had in five years.

"I think there is no case for postponement of elections at all," he said in an interview with Reuters. Measures to bring corrupt people to account and prevent loan defaulters or tax evaders from standing in the polls would weed out "rascals".
Election spending would be curtailed and candidates screened to stop "people with dubious wealth and dubious financial resources" from standing, but there would be no victimisation.

"So an element that was creeping in our politics of black money, of illegal money, or drug money financing political candidates would by and large be removed. These are not insiginificant changes," the president declared.

He said about 6,000 Pakistanis had defaulted on bank loans worth more than 500,000 rupees ($12,430), but it was not known how many of them planned to run for parliament. They would have to repay their loans first in order to qualify.
"The accountability system and the appeal to the electorate should take care of the rascals," he said.

Leghari set the election date in line with the constitution after using controversial powers to dissolve the National Assembly (lower house) and sack Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
He said the government had decided on Thursday to grant an estimated two million people in Pakistan's semi-autonomous tribal areas full voting rights for the first time.

"We have done something which is very revolutionary and which has extended democracy in Pakistan's last remaining bastion which was outside the adult franchise system -- the tribal area of Pakistan," he said.
In the past, the tribal areas near the Afghan border had elected eight members of the National Assembly (lower house), who in turn elected eight members of the Senate (upper house).
The National Assembly members were elected by electoral colleges with memberships ranging from 1,600 to 3,200 voters.

"Now the electoral college will consist of every adult citizen of Pakistan living in those areas above the age of 21 years," Leghari said. "Almost all political parties had been promising this over the last 40 to 50 years. We have done that."

He accused Bhutto and her detained spouse, Asif Ali Zardari, of being corrupt and did not rule out the possibility of murder charges being brought against Zardari in connection with the September 20 killing of Bhutto's estranged brother Murtaza.
He dismissed as "ridiculous" Bhutto's charge that he himself was responsible for the death of her brother, killed by a hail of police bullets in Karachi along with seven companions.

Leghari said world leaders and newspapers had not criticised his action in sacking his former party ally. "They all said Benazir had it coming because she and her spouse were indulging in mal-governance, in corruption on a massive scale," he said.

Leghari said he planned to announce economic reforms later this month that would lay the groundwork for an agreement with the International Monetary Fund on a long-term lending programme known as an enhanced structural adjustment facility.

Shahid Javed Burki, finance and economic affairs adviser to the prime minister, was due to meet the IMF board in Washington on Friday ahead of an expected release of at least $160 million in delayed tranches of Pakistan's $600 million standby loan.
Leghari said the caretakers had inherited a disastrous economic situation, but had stopped the rot.
"We had a very bad spectacle of having...respected organisations such as Transparency International calling Pakistan the second or third most corrupt country in the world."

"We were in great danger of flight of capital. Confidence in our economy had eroded. The credibility of the government...had eroded to a point where people had started looking at Pakistan as a very dangerous and dubious case," he said.
Leghari said the interim government aimed to rebuild foreign reserves to over $1 billion by the end of December, and to $1.5 billion by election time, from $590 million when it took office.
"So by the time the new elected government takes place, they would have an economy which has stabilised," he said.
"I think the caretakers have done more work in these five weeks than governments in the past have done in five years."
